title: Firearm experts close Crown evidence at OPP officer's manslaughter trial
article: Two firearms experts were the final two Crown witnesses as a Chatham-Kent OPP officer's manslaughter trial continued Wednesday.
Veteran Const. Sean O'Rourke, 57, has pleaded not guilty in the July 2021 shooting death of Nicholas Edward Grieves, 24, of Brantford.
O'Rourke and Sgt. Bradley Cook were responding to a reported gas theft from the Dutton ONroute rest stop on Highway 401 about 4:30 a.m. on July 7, 2021, court has heard.

Grieves was shot in the right shoulder after his westbound 2003 Pontiac Sunfire went off the road into the centre median near Highgate after O'Rourke and Cook initiated a "tandem stop" using their cruisers, court has heard. The bullet severed two main arteries and Grieves died later in hospital.
Judy Chin, a firearms expert with the Centre of Forensic Sciences in Toronto, testified about her examination of O'Rourke's Glock Model 17 semi-automatic pistol, OPP officers' standard-issue firearm.
Crown attorney Jason Nicol asked if she found any structural or operational defects. "Not according to my notes," Chin said.
Tests found it took an average of 9.926 pounds of force to pull the gun's trigger, which was on the "heavier side" of average, she said.
Asked if the gun could fire without someone pulling the trigger, Chin replied: "For this firearm, the trigger must be pulled, but it doesn't have to be pulled by a person."

On cross-examination, Chin told defence lawyer Sandy Khehra she did not examine the weapon under a microscope for damage or conduct a drop or bump test, which might cause the weapon to accidentally discharge.
OPP Insp. Jason Oxby was qualified for the first time as an expert witness on OPP firearm training policies and procedures.
Asked by Nicol to explain the threshold for an officer drawing their firearm, Oxby said there needs to be a "threat of serious bodily harm or death to self or someone else."
The OPP's position when it comes to drawing a firearm is "it's up to the member to make that decision," he said. "The circumstances can be very dynamic."
When a weapon is drawn, the officer must keep their finger off the trigger until ready to fire, he added.
Khera asked if an officer was "permitted to point their weapon in the direction of the subject even if they haven't made the decision to shoot."
Khehra also asked about training scenarios for using the weapon-mounted light on the Glock pistol in dark and low-light situations, and the two ways the light can be activated.
